text: On 27 November 43 BC, the Lex Titia initiated the period of absolute rule at Rome.
Antony, Lepidus and Octavian were charged with 'restoring the state', as triumviri rei publicae constituendae, a board of three men with power to set the state in order.
The three had the power to make or annul laws without consulting Senate or people.
They had the power to exercise jurisdiction without any right of appeal.
They had the power to nominate magistrates of their choice.
Antony received Cisalpine Gaul and Further Gaul.
Lepidus received Narbonensis and Spain.
Octavian received Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica.
Lepidus was included among the three, and Plancus and Pollio were not.
Pollio was to be in the region, and he too had veterans under his command.
Octavian took over Gaul bloodlessly on Calenus' death in 40 BC.
In 6 BC the people 'chose' Gaius as consul, and Augustus stepped in and quashed it.
In the year 6 BC Tiberius Nero received a renewal of imperium, plus tribunician power for five years.
In 5 BC Gaius was made a pontifex, a member of the chief college of priests.
In 5 BC Gaius was designated consul for AD 1.
A new title was invented for Gaius, princeps iuventutis or honorary president of the order of equites.
In 2 BC Lucius was made an augur, a priest who read the signs of the gods.
In 2 BC Lucius was designated consul for AD 4.
Lucius became joint princeps iuventutis.
In 4 BC a senatus consultum, on a proposal from Augustus, made a new, expedited procedure available to provincials alleging extortion by Roman magistrates.
Augustus had taken the consulship in 5 BC to preside over the debut of Gaius Caesar.
In 2 BC Augustus was consul ordinarius, to preside over the debut of Lucius.
On 5 February 2 BC Augustus was officially designated pater patriae, 'Father of the Nation'.
One of them had been consul, one of the two chief magistrates elected each year, in 9 BC.
As praetor, a magistrate ranked below the consuls who judged cases, Iullus gave the games for Augustus' birthday in 13 BC.
Iullus reached the consulship in 10 BC.
In 2 BC prefects of the praetorian guard, commanders of the ruler's guard, were appointed for the first time.
dispute: Some historians link the new prefects to an alleged state of emergency; the page doubts it.

text: The first prefects were a pair, and both were equites.

In 2 BC the suffect consuls, consuls who took office in place of others during the year, Lucius Caninius Gallus and Gaius Fufius Geminus, put through the comitia a law setting limits to the number of slaves an individual master might free by will.
In 1 BC Gaius Caesar was invested with an imperium for the whole East.
In AD 1 Gaius entered in absentia upon his long-prearranged consulship.
In AD 3 Augustus' constitutional powers were renewed for a full decade.
In AD 3 there was no collega imperii.
In AD 4 Tiberius Nero received tribunician power, the powers of a tribune of the plebs, held without the office, for ten years.
dispute: Suetonius gives a different term; the page says Suetonius is wrong.

text: In AD 4 Tiberius Nero was appointed to command in Germany.
dispute: He apparently did not hold a general imperium maius; the page is not certain.

text: Proconsuls, governors of a province with a consul's powers, had to be appointed instead of chosen by the lot.
The tenures of proconsuls were prolonged.
Sardinia was redesignated as a part of the 'province of Caesar' because of a recrudescence of the corsairs.
A new fire service, the vigiles, was established under an equestrian prefect, a commander drawn from the equites.
In AD 7 Germanicus was quaestor, a junior magistrate who handled public money.
In AD 7 Germanicus was sent to Illyricum with troop reinforcements for Tiberius.
Augustus nominated all the magistrates himself, the only time he did so.
Augustus appointed a committee of senior senators to take over the hearing of embassies.
Marion was tyrant of Tyre.
Full triumphs were voted to Augustus and Tiberius.
Germanicus was voted ornamenta triumphalia.
Germanicus was given permission to stand for the consulship, one of the two chief magistracies of the state, held for a year, ahead of normal.
Tiberius took on Germany.
In AD 12 Germanicus was consul.
In AD 13 the constitutional powers of Augustus and Tiberius were renewed again for ten years.
In AD 13 the imperium of Tiberius was declared equal to that of Augustus.
dispute: The notes say there can be no certainty just when Tiberius received that grant.

text: Tiberius was collega imperii, a colleague holding command equal to the ruler's.
dispute: The notes say there can be no certainty just when Tiberius received that grant.

text: The senatorial sub-committee that prepared business for the full Senate was given a revised membership.
The sub-committee was given new powers to pass resolutions equivalent to formal senatus consulta.
Tiberius, Germanicus and Drusus joined the sub-committee as regular members.
The senators then decided to keep the death-duty.
Augustus and Tiberius began a census, with a special grant of consular imperium.
From 30 BC, the whole Roman world was in the grasp of a single ruler, Augustus.
Augustus possessed all power and made all decisions, except those he chose to leave to others.
Tacitus wrote that Augustus paraded himself as consul, one of the two chief magistrates of Rome, elected each year.
Tacitus wrote that Augustus was content with the tribunician authority, the powers of a tribune of the commons, held without the post, for looking after the commons.
Tacitus wrote that Augustus edged forward bit by bit, taking into his hands the functions of Senate, magistrates, laws.
Augustus held actual coercive power totally from the start and never let a particle of it slip from his hands.
Augustus' ultimate possibility of coercion lay in control of the army.
The Senate allotted armies to those whose provinciae required them.
The troops swore an oath of obedience to each commander set to lead them.
In the first years after 30 BC, Augustus was consul.
From 27 BC, the provincia given to Augustus entitled him to overall command of the troops within it.
Most of the troops were in that provincia, and their oath of obedience was to Augustus.
For a time, independent proconsuls continued with their own auspicia.
Those proconsuls did not command enough forces to be a serious counterpoise to those commanded by Augustus.
Augustus' formal powers gave him the right to choose his legati, deputies who commanded troops and governed in his name, for his provincia.
Augustus' provincia included most of the areas of military activity.
The imperium that Augustus caused to be bestowed on himself gave him the formal right to receive out of public revenue the cost of the major part of the armies.
Augustus nominated as he chose to the new executive posts he created, such as the praetorian prefectures, command of the guard that protected the ruler.
Augustus appointed whom he chose as overall commanders of the main enterprises.
Augustus took over responsibility for food supply, security and fire-fighting in the capital.
Antony recognized Herod and his brother Phasael as 'tetrarchs'.
The crown-prince, the heir to the throne, Pacorus and Q. Labienus shared the Parthian command.
At the end of his Geography, Strabo asserts that Augustus received 'headship of the hegemony' and 'the power of war and peace for life'.
dispute: The page holds that Strabo is not making a constitutional statement.

text: That division was made, in all probability, in a senatorial debate, not by any overriding power of Augustus.
dispute: The page says this is probable, not certain.

text: The laudation records that Agrippa received tribunician power for five years in 18 BC on the basis of a senatus consultum, and again in 13 BC.
The laudation records a statute 'that no man's authority should be greater than yours in any province to which the public weal of Rome might hale you'.
Instead he put bills before the comitia by virtue of his tribunician power.
Augustus could summon the Senate and put motions to it.
The resulting decisions were senatus consulta.
Labienus styled himself Q. LABIENUS PARTHICUS IMPERATOR.
evidence: coins (EJ2 8, RRC 524); Strab. 14.2.24-5; Plut. Ant. 28.1; Dio 48.26.5
dispute: Plutarch and Strabo read the title as 'commander of the Parthians'; Dio reads Parthicus as a surname Labienus took after his troops hailed him imperator.

text: Pacorus installed the pretender Antigonus on the throne.
Antony's brother L. Antonius was consul in 41 BC.
Calenus never gave the promised two legions.
In all, thirteen Antonian legions stood by, inactive.
L. Antonius himself had no more than eight legions.
Antonius was sent to govern Spain.
Octavian occupied Gaul.
After this, Sextus occupied Sardinia.
Sextus displaced Octavian's governor, the official who ran a province, M. Lurius.
The consul Pollio persuaded Domitius Ahenobarbus to join Antony.
Brundisium was guarded by five of Octavian's legions.
The agreement closely duplicated the compact of Philippi, except for the change that followed from Calenus' death.
Octavian's occupation of Gaul was recognized.
The treaty gave Octavian Illyricum as well.
Antony was recognized as master of the East.
Antony controlled the East and Octavian the West.
Scodra in Illyria was made the dividing-point of the dominions.
The treaty let Lepidus retain Africa.
The consulships for the next few years were allocated.
The legions were reallocated.
Italy was supposed to be shared by both men, open to each for his recruiting.
Sextus had taken over Corsica as well.
Salvidienus Rufus was consul designate, consul designate, a man elected consul who had not yet taken office, for the following year.
Octavian recalled his general Salvidienus Rufus from Gaul.
The senatus consultum ultimum was passed to prepare the killing of Salvidienus.
A dispensation for the marriage was secured from the Senate.
Antony and Octavian agreed that Herod should be recognized as king, king, a monarch who ruled a kingdom, of Judaea.
The formal decision on Herod was deferred to the Senate.
During 39 BC the triumvirs secured a senatorial decree to ratify all their acts, both those already done and those not yet done.
evidence: App. BCiv. 5.75.518; Dio 48.34.1; an inscription, Reynolds 1982 doc. 8

text: Sextus was to retain Corsica as well as Sicily and Sardinia.
Sextus was also to take the Peloponnese.
Sextus was to hold this dominion for five years.
Consulships were agreed for every year till 32 BC.
Libo was promised the consulship of 34 BC.
Sextus was promised the consulship of 33 BC, just after the expiry of his quinquennium.
For the present, Sextus was given an augurship, augur, a priest who read the will of the gods from signs.
By the autumn of 39 BC the Senate rewarded Stratoniceia and Aphrodisias-Plarasa for their resistance to Labienus.
Antony reversed the process, weakening the cities and establishing a new strong kingdom of Pontus.
The kingdom of Pontus was to be ruled by Darius.
The possessions of Deiotarus in Pontus were assigned to Darius.
Castor, the grandson of Deiotarus, was recognized as king of Galatia.
Castor was also allowed the interior of Paphlagonia.
Lysanias was confirmed as king of Ituraea.
Amyntas was given Pisidia.
Polemo received a dominion combining the western part of Cilicia with some parts of Lycaonia.
The realm of Polemo extended as far as Iconium.
Cleopatra was given Cyprus and a region of eastern Cilicia.
evidence: Strab. 14.5.2-3; an inscription naming an Egyptian official of 'Cyprus and Cilicia' in 38-7
dispute: The page says this probably happened at this time, not certainly.

text: Antony arrived to take over the campaign.
The triumvirate had formally expired at the end of 38 BC.
The triumvirs had not abdicated.
Sextus was stripped of his priesthood and his promised consulship.
The dictatorships, a magistracy holding supreme power in an emergency, of Sulla and Caesar had been voted without any time-limitation.
Caesar's dictatorship had at first been annual.
It had then been formally extended to ten years.
It had then been made 'for life'.
Caesar's command in Gaul had been assigned by a law (lex) rather than by a decree of the Senate (s.c).
That command had carried a fixed term.
In November 43 BC the triumvirs needed a lex to establish them in office.
The triumvirs assigned their provincial commands to themselves by virtue of their triumviral powers.
They also had those commands ratified by a decree of the Senate (s.c).
It was not clear whether the triumvirs' provincial imperium lapsed when their triumviral powers lapsed.
dispute: The page says this was not at all clear.

text: In 37 BC the triumvirate was formally renewed for another five years.
The renewed term very probably expired on the last day of 33 BC.
dispute: The page says only 'very probably'; an endnote discusses the date.

text: Agrippa was consul, one of the two chief magistrates elected each year, in 37 BC.
In 39 BC Polemo held a small dominion.
Two legions were sent ahead under Herod's direct command.
Orodes abdicated.
dispute: The page gives the date only as late 38 or 37.

text: C. Sosius was Antony's governor, the commander and administrator of a province, of Syria (in modern Syria) and Cilicia.
Herod became king, a monarch ruling a kingdom.
The East was divided into a number of large client kingdoms, each ruled by a prince.
Castor's son Deiotarus was allowed to inherit Paphlagonia.
dispute: He possibly held it at first jointly with his elder brother Deiotarus Philopator.

text: Galatia passed to Amyntas.
Amyntas's realm was greatly expanded to include parts of Pamphylia and Polemo's former domain in Lycaonia.
By 37-36 BC Archelaus was confirmed as king of Cappadocia.
The priest-kings, rulers who were also chief priests of a temple state, in southern Pontus, at Comana, Megalopolis and Zela (in modern Zile, Turkey), were retained and strengthened.
Cleon was created a prince in Mysia.
Adiatorix was created a prince in Heraclea Pontica.
In Upper Cilicia Tarcondimotus was encouraged in his small kingdom.
In 37-36 BC Cleopatra was given parts of coastal Phoenicia and Nabataean Arabia (in modern Jordan).
dispute: Plut. and Dio place these grants in 37-36; Joseph. AJ 15.94-5 appears to place the gifts of parts of Phoenicia, Arabia and Judaea in 34, but the notes judge that he combines several phases.

text: In 37-36 BC Cleopatra was also given the rich balsam woods around Jericho (in modern Jericho) in Judaea.
dispute: Joseph. AJ 15.94-5 appears to place the gift of parts of Judaea in 34.

text: Cleopatra took over his kingdom along with some adjoining territory.
evidence: Porphyry FGrH 260 F 2.17; Dio 49.32.5; Joseph. AJ 15.92, BJ 1.440
dispute: The adjoining territory probably included Canatha, Hippos and Gadara, and possibly Damascus, where Cleopatra's portrait appears on coins.

text: Cleopatra perhaps had her dominion in Cilicia extended.
dispute: The page says only 'perhaps'.

text: Cleopatra became mistress of Crete and Cyrene.
dispute: The page says this happened now or earlier.

text: In Armenia Antony linked with Canidius' army, perhaps at the plateau of Erzerum, perhaps at Artaxata.
dispute: The place is uncertain; scholars differ between Erzerum and Artaxata.

text: Contingents from the allied kings, including Polemo, joined Antony.
Antony had perhaps sixteen legions and a mass of auxiliaries.
dispute: The page gives the figure only as 'perhaps'.

text: Artavasdes of Armenia supplied a large contingent of cataphracts and lighter-armed cavalry, perhaps as many as 16,000.
dispute: Plutarch elsewhere gives '6,000' at the initial muster, and another source gives 6,000 cataphracts 'besides the other cavalry'; the figures may differ between the muster and later arrivals, or between paper strength and the force that came.

text: At first there was one pair of consuls, the highest magistracy, for the entire year, on the traditional republican pattern.
The number of consulships each year and the choice of holders quickly came to be for the emperor alone to decide.
From 5 BC the two 'ordinary' consuls, who opened the year, were regularly replaced by one or two further pairs of 'suffect' consuls at variable intervals.
Up to six men could thus hold the consulship within a single year.
Certain highly distinguished men held a second, and even a third, consulship.
Before 23 BC Augustus was always consul and frequently out of Rome.
After 23 BC he was given the right to bring forward one item at any stage of any meeting.
He was also given authority to summon the Senate as often as he pleased.
In theory he could already summon it by virtue of his tribunicia potestas.
In 19 BC he was granted the right to sit on the president's tribunal at meetings, between the two consuls.
These privileges were conferred upon subsequent emperors on their accession.
dispute: The page infers this ('must have been').

text: In AD 13, the decisions of the consilium were granted authority equal to that of the full Senate.
Augustus derived his formal authority from the Senate.
The resolutions of the Senate came to be recognized as law without confirmation by a popular assembly.
The Senate bestowed honours in greater quantity and variety than ever.
The authority of the Senate in matters of religion was still accepted as supreme.
The emperor reserved to himself matters relating to the army and foreign affairs.
The emperor reserved to himself public finance.
The Senate lost the prerogative of determining the disposition of the state's military forces year by year and the extent of the territory to which it laid claim.
Augustus arranged for these new officials to be appointed by the Senate.
Augustus arranged for the activities of these officials to be authorized by the Senate.
In the early weeks of the reign of Tiberius, elections to magistracies were transferred to the Senate from the popular assemblies.
dispute: The page says it is obscure how far the change was an idea of Augustus rather than of Tiberius; the timing was decided by Tiberius.

text: This time Lepidus came in force.
Lepidus arrived with twelve legions and 5,000 cavalry.
Octavian had twenty-one legions on the island, besides Lepidus' army.
Sextus had only ten legions.
Agrippa, not Octavian, took command.
Plinius Rufus had command of eight legions of Sextus' army.
Lepidus remained pontifex maximus, the chief priest of the state cults.
Octavian took over Africa and Sicily into his own domain.
After the fall of Sextus, Octavian had forty-five legions.
Octavian's other honours included a grant of tribunicial sacrosanctity.
Calvisius Sabinus was appointed to put down Italian brigandage.
evidence: App. BCiv. v.132.547; cf. Suet. Aug. 32; Dio XLIX.15.1

text: In 33 BC nearly all Antony's legions were still in the extreme east of his domain.
In 49 BC the legions serving under Caesar in Gaul were numbered in a set sequence from V to XIV.
These legions formed the basis of Caesar's army thereafter.
Caesar held the consulship, one of the two chief magistracies of the Roman state, held for a year, in 48 BC.
All but a few of these legions had been raised or reconstituted under Caesar's direct command.
These legions formed the backbone of the triumviral army, the triumvirs were three men who held joint power over the state, for the Philippi campaign.
Some of the most senior of the Antonian legions were accepted intact into Octavian's army.
Octavian continued to recruit auxiliaries from the western provinces under his control.
In the East, Pompey, the Liberators and Antony drew on the armies of client kings in Thrace, Asia Minor, Syria, Judaea and Egypt.
At Actium, Antony embarked 20,000 legionaries, that is four legions, for the battle.
At Actium, Octavian placed eight legions on his ships.
Octavian also placed five praetorian cohorts on his ships.
Most legions were in provinces controlled by Augustus himself through his legates.
Augustus began to appoint legates directly to command a specific legion.
Such a legate held office with the title legatus legionis (legionary legate) for a period of several years.
An equestrian officer with the title praefectus castrorum (prefect of the camp) was appointed to supervise the running of each legion's permanent base-camp.
In Egypt command of a legion fell to the praefectus castrorum.
At the end Sextus had little more than three legions and a handful of ships.
Antony appointed M. Titius to take charge of the problem of Sextus.
By the spring of 35 BC the pursuit was tying up the governors, a magistrate ruling a province, of both Asia and Bithynia, C. Furnius and Domitius Ahenobarbus.
In AD 7 Tiberius mustered ten legions, more than seventy cohorts, and ten alae at Sirmium.
In AD 9 Varus marched in Germany with six cohorts of infantry and three alae of cavalry, in addition to his three legions.
Regiments of auxilia were commanded by prefects, with the title praefectus cohortis for infantry or praefectus equitum for an ala of cavalry.
Where Roman officers were appointed as prefects, these were often centurions of substantial military experience, especially primipilares (former chief centurions of a legion).
Other Roman prefects were men of equestrian rank, often former tribunes in a legion.
Herod used Roman officers to command his forces.
The commanders of these citizen cohorts were styled tribunes.
Individual ships were commanded by trierarchs.
Squadrons were commanded by navarchs.
Each of the major fleets was commanded by a praefectus classis.
The fleet-prefects at this time were usually ex-legionary tribunes or ex-chief centurions.
After Philippi Octavian and Antony retained 8,000 time-served veterans who rejected the proffered land-allotments, to serve as praetorians.
Before Actium there is a report that Antony had three cohorts.
At Actium Octavian had five cohorts present.
dispute: The size of these cohorts is uncertain.

text: After Actium Octavian continued to employ cohortes praetoriae, which became a permanent 'household division'.
The cohorts were attached to the military headquarters (praetorium) which Octavian maintained as a proconsul.
In 2 BC Augustus appointed two equestrians as praefecti praetorio, prefects of the praetorium.
The cohortes vigilum were under an equestrian praefectus vigilum.
evidence: Dio LV.26.4; Strab. V.3.7 (234-5C); Suet. Aug. 25.2

text: The cohortes vigilum were officered by tribunes who had been chief centurions of a legion.
The force remained in being until it was disbanded by Galba.
The triumvirs controlled appointments to the consulship, the highest yearly magistracy at Rome, and to many of the lower offices.
Antony left his troops in Armenia for the winter.
Within a year at least sixteen legions were in Armenia.
Antony declared Cleopatra monarch, along with her son Caesarion, of Egypt, Cyprus and Koile Syria.
Armenia, Media and, when conquered, Parthia were to fall to their six-year-old son Alexander Helios.
Libya and Cyrene were to fall to his twin Cleopatra Selene.
Ptolemy Philadelphus, still only two, was to have Phoenicia, Syria and Cilicia.
The association of Caesarion in the monarchy was not new.
The Antonian consuls, the two chief magistrates of the year, Sosius and Ahenobarbus aimed to hush up the affair of the Donations, some fifteen months earlier.
In 35 BC sacrosanctity was extended to include Octavia.
A recent mutiny had shown that Octavian's control of the veterans was insecure.
At the same time an army of Octavian was apparently active somewhere in Illyricum.
evidence: App. BCiv. v.80.538; Vell. Pat. ii.78.2
dispute: It is possible, but not very likely, that Octavian's army and Pollio's were one and the same.

text: In 33 BC Agrippa was aedile, a Roman magistrate who cared for the city's buildings, streets, supplies and games.
All, or almost all, of Antony's eastern army, sixteen legions, was in Armenia.
Antony gave Lesser Armenia to Polemo.
The triumvirate, by now a duovirate, was not renewed.
The consuls of 32 BC were C. Sosius and Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus.
Antony did not legally need this ratification, because all the triumviral acts had been ratified in advance.
On 1 February Sosius took over the fasces and launched a public attack on Octavian.
dispute: Some scholars hold that Sosius launched his attack on 1 January.

text: A tribune, an officer elected to protect the people, with power to veto, vetoed Sosius' motion of censure.
dispute: The page says it is uncertain whether the motion would otherwise have passed; the veto may have been arranged beforehand.

text: Antony and Octavian were to share the command in the campaign against Brutus and Cassius in the East.
The triumvirs controlled forty-three legions.
Lepidus was to remain in control of Italy.
Two partisans of Antony were to stay, Calenus in Italy and Pollio in the Cisalpina, both with strong armies.
Early in 42 BC a preliminary force of eight triumviral legions, under C. Norbanus and L. Decidius Saxa, crossed the Adriatic.
The Liberators' fleets began to operate in the Adriatic, some 130 ships under L. Staius Murcus and Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus.
By early 42 BC he had established himself in control of Sicily.
Antony organized the senators who had fled into a 'countersenate'.
Antony's army was more than 100,000 strong.
Titius was consul designate, a man elected to hold the consulship, one of the two chief yearly magistracies, in a coming year.
dispute: The notes say he may first have been designated for a different year.

text: Antony still called himself triumvir.
The Res Gestae spoke of more than 700 senators 'serving under Octavian's colours'.
dispute: The phrase is often taken to mean that all the senators went with Octavian on campaign; the notes say that need not follow.

text: Antony was stripped of the consulship he was to hold in 31 BC.
Antony was also stripped of 'the rest of his power'.
dispute: The page takes this to mean the triumvirate, which Antony still claimed; whether he still held it depends on one's view.

text: The largest of these battles was won by Statilius Taurus and Titius, by then one of Octavian's commanders.
Four legions under L. Pinarius Scarpus stayed in Cyrene.
Between them they controlled probably twenty-one legions.
dispute: The page gives this number as probable, not certain.

text: By the end of 31 BC, Octavian had taken over Asia Minor.
Q. Didius was Octavian's governor of Syria.
Cornelius Gallus had taken over and reinforced Pinarius' legions.
The Lex Titia of 27 November 43 BC established the triumvirate, a board of three men holding power together, for five years.
The first term of the triumvirate ended on 31 December, five years and a little over a month after it began.
The triumvirate was renewed for a further term at the conference of Tarentum in 37 BC.
Antony and Octavian were due to assume the consulship, the chief yearly magistracy, on 1 January 31 BC.
Augustus claimed to have held the triumvirate "per continuos annos decem".
dispute: The endnote reads this as 27 November 43 BC to 31 December 33 BC, against Appian's reckoning.

text: At Tarentum the triumvirs backdated the new term to 1 January 37 BC.
dispute: The terminal date of the new term is disputed.

text: At Misenum the triumvirs completed their consular lists for the following years.
At Misenum they fixed on 31 BC rather than 32 BC as the date for their own consulship.
The Antonians Ahenobarbus and Sosius were due to be consuls in 32 BC.
In 36 BC the people voted Octavian "protection from insult in word or deed".
dispute: Appian and Orosius say Octavian received tribunicia potestas in 36 BC; the endnote holds that Dio is right that he received only sacrosanctity then.

text: Anyone who committed such an outrage was to fall liable to "the same penalties as in the case of a tribune", an officer of the people whose person was sacrosanct.
In 36 BC Octavian also received the right to sit on the tribunician bench.
In the following year sacrosanctity was extended to Octavia and Livia.
Appian wrote that in 36 BC 'they' elected Octavian tribune for ever.
dispute: The endnote judges this a misinterpretation; Dio XLIX.15.5-6 records only sacrosanctity in 36 BC.

text: Orosius attested a grant of full tribunicia potestas to Octavian in 36 BC.
dispute: The endnote judges this a misinterpretation; Dio XLIX.15.5-6 records only sacrosanctity in 36 BC.

text: Norbanus and Saxa fell back upon Amphipolis, where they linked with the main army under Antony.
Caesar now had all the power there was.
Its governor was an eques, a member of the order of knights, the rank below senators, not a senator.
At Rome the eques Gaius Maecenas held tight control on behalf of the absent Caesar.
Valid consuls were in office at the time.
In 30 BC the absent Caesar was voted the 'Vote of Athena', the power of pardon.
He was voted the auxilii latio, the power, like a tribune, an officer who could come to the aid of citizens against magistrates, to come to the aid of citizens in the city of Rome.
dispute: Dio says he was given all the powers of a tribune for life; the notes say that may have been offered, and that Caesar accepted only 'most' of what was offered.

text: He was voted the power to 'judge when called upon'.
dispute: Scholars use this power to seek a constitutional basis for the emperor as judge; the page sees these powers as marks of honour or as giving him judicial standing in the East.

text: Caesar entered upon his fourth consulship, the year before 29 BC, while away from Rome.
Caesar entered upon his fifth consulship of 29 BC while still in the East.
At its first meeting of 29 BC the Senate granted Caesar the right to use Imperator as his permanent first name.
evidence: coins (he already used the name in fact on coins in the triumviral period)

text: The Senate gave formal approval to his eastern diplomatic arrangements.
Caesar and Agrippa were granted censoria potestas, the authority of censors, magistrates who took the census of citizens and revised the senate-list.
In 28 BC Caesar and Agrippa were both consules ordinarii of the year.
Dio records a new rule that senators might leave Italy-Sicily only with Caesar's permission.
His sixth consulship was in 28 BC and his seventh in 27 BC.
dispute: The page holds that the change ran across both years and was no single 'constitutional settlement of 27 B.C.'

text: In 28 BC Caesar shared the consular fasces month by month with his colleague, in the traditional manner.
At the beginning of 27 B.C. Caesar and Agrippa were joint consuls, one of the two yearly chief magistrates of the Roman state, once again.
The Senate granted Caesar a provincia, a sphere of command given to a magistrate.
dispute: The page thinks the Senate's response was prepared in advance; a footnote cites Dio LIII.11 as against that view.

text: That provincia, 'Caesar's province', was Spain, Gaul and Syria.
Egypt was also in Caesar's province.
Caesar's province was granted on a ten-year maximum tenure.
Caesar made no gesture to resign the consulship.
Caesar could hold his provincia either as consul or as proconsul, a governor holding a consul's power outside the city.
No change was made in the traditional arrangements for the rest of the provinces of the Roman world.
Strabo states that at this time Caesar received 'headship of the hegemony' and was made arbiter of peace and war for life.
dispute: The author gives reasons for limiting the significance of Strabo's claim.

text: Caesar resigned the consulship in July 23 BC.
Cassius commanded the left, facing Antony.
Brutus commanded the right, facing Octavian.
Crassus was consul ordinarius, a consul who took office at the start of the year, in 30 B.C.
Gallus was first prefect of Egypt, the governor of Egypt, chosen from the equites.
The Senate declared that Gallus was liable to prosecution.
Augustus continued to entrust Egypt to equites.
Augustus did not let the prefects of Egypt rise further.
The war was carried forward by legates, deputies who command for a governor.
Augustus' consular colleagues in Rome in 27 and 26 BC were Marcus Agrippa and Titus Statilius Taurus.
In 26 BC, from Spain, Augustus appointed a prefect of the city, an official who saw to the government of the city when the consuls were absent.
The prefect of the city was the triumphator Messalla Corvinus.
In 26 BC there was a sitting consul.
Messalla accepted the post and gave it up after six days.
evidence: Tac. Ann. VI.11; Sen. Apocol. 10; Jerome, Chron. sub ann. 26
dispute: The sources differ on why: Tacitus says he claimed he did not understand the job-description; Seneca says he was embarrassed by the job; Jerome calls it an unconstitutional position. Scholars also differ.

text: According to Tacitus, Statilius Taurus took the post, and with success.
dispute: The page says he hardly took it immediately, for he was consul.

text: Agrippa held the aedileship, a magistracy that oversaw the city and its games, in 33 B.C.
Augustus entered on his tenth consulship on the road from Spain to Rome, on 1 January 24 B.C.
On 1 January 24 B.C. the Senate took an oath to uphold Augustus' acta.
According to Dio, the Senate 'released him from all compulsion of the laws', which meant Augustus was to be 'master of himself and the laws and do what he liked and not do what he did not like'.
dispute: The author treats the alleged grant as a proposal made in Augustus' absence that never got beyond the Senate.

text: In 24 B.C. Marcellus was admitted to the Senate with the rank of one who had already held the praetorship, the magistracy next below the consulship.
In 24 BC Tiberius was elected quaestor, the lowest regular magistracy, chiefly financial, for 23 BC.
In 23 BC Marcellus was made aedile.
Dio remarks elsewhere that the emperor is 'absolved from the laws'.
After his recovery a law was passed conferring upon Agrippa an imperium proconsulare, a governor's power of command.
evidence: Augustus' funeral oration for Agrippa, EJ2 366

text: Agrippa's imperium was not maius.
Agrippa governed Syria through his own legates.
On 1 July 23 B.C. Augustus laid down his eleventh consulship.
Augustus had held one place of the consulship for years.
Agrippa had twice held the other place.
Augustus received the grant of the official powers possessed by tribunes of the plebs, officers elected to protect the common people, tribunicia potestas.
The grant was annually renewable but for life.
Augustus used the tribunician power to summon the Senate and to introduce legislation.
Tribunicia potestas was a bundle of specifically defined powers.
dispute: Some historians call the tribunician power 'vague' and 'all-embracing'; the page disagrees with them.

text: The Senate granted Augustus the right to make a formal motion at any session.
The imperium of Augustus was redefined as imperium maius.
Imperium maius gave him prevailing authority over any other provincial governor, a magistrate who ruled a province, in any case of conflict.
It was only proconsular imperium, giving him no authority in the home sphere such as he had possessed as consul, one of the two highest magistrates of the state, elected each year.
He was allowed to have it 'once for all', without dropping it every time he entered the sacred pomerium of Rome and resuming it every time he departed.
The redefinition kept Augustus' imperium one stage higher than the new imperium of Agrippa.
dispute: Some read the redefinition as making up to Augustus for the maius imperium consuls had held; historians are not agreed that consuls held such power in practice.

text: Marcus Primus, proconsul, the governor of a province, holding a consul's powers, of Macedonia, was tried for making war on the Odrysae of Thrace unprovoked and without authority.
dispute: The page says the trial has been moved by some to 23 BC; it places it in 22 BC.

text: The Senate, under heavy pressure from the city plebs, offered him the dictatorship, an emergency magistracy with supreme power.
dispute: Augustus says in his own record that it was offered twice.

text: He was offered the powers of a censor, a magistrate who kept the list of citizens and judged their conduct, for life.
He was offered a consulship, 'annual yet perpetual', like his tribunician power.
Augustus accepted cura annonae, charge of the corn supply.
A new annual committee of senior senators, praefecti frumenti dandi, senators charged with handing out the free corn, was set up to improve the distribution of the free ration.
No prefect of the city, an official who kept order in the city while the ruler was away, was appointed.
The people in comitia refused to elect more than one consul for 21 BC.
Augustus, writing from Samos, refused to take the vacant place.
Only at the beginning of 21 BC did the people elect a second consul.
In 20 BC the comitia again declined to elect more than one consul, Gaius Sentius Saturninus.
In early 19 BC Gaius Sentius Saturninus faced, alone, the rise of a 'people's champion', Marcus Egnatius Rufus.
As aedile, a magistrate in charge of city services and public games, he won the favour of the Roman plebs by organizing a fire service.
dispute: The sources are muddled, not least in their dates.

text: That took him straight to the praetorship, the magistracy next below the consulship, chiefly in charge of the law courts.
A popular uprising was suppressed in accordance with a senatus consultum ultimum.
In the new division of power, Antony was to organize the East.
Antony was to retain Further Gaul and take Narbonensis from Lepidus.
Antony lost the Cisalpina, which was to become part of Italy.
Octavian was to retain Sardinia and take both provinces of Spain from Lepidus.
Lepidus was allowed only Africa.
evidence: App. BCiv. V.5.12; Dio XLVIII.1.3; Dio XLVIII.22.2
dispute: The sources suggest some doubt even about Africa.

text: Antony was to take six of these legions, and Octavian five.
Octavian was to lend Antony a further two legions.
In the West, Antony's marshals seem to have controlled about as many legions as Octavian.
dispute: The page says the position concerning the western legions is obscure.

text: Antony promised that Calenus would transfer to Octavian two legions in Italy.
The legions stayed with Calenus.
The governor of Gaul was to be Calenus, with eleven legions.
It was done by the authority of his imperium maius.
Augustus appointed, proprio motu, a second consul for the empty place.
Dio lists a grant to Augustus in 19 BC of an 'overseership of morality'.
dispute: Augustus' own record says he refused a magistracy of curator morum (RG 6.1, Greek only); the page holds that the offer was rejected.

text: Dio lists a censorial authority among the grants of 19 BC.
dispute: The notes say refusal of censorial power is implied in RG 8; the page holds that the offer was rejected.

text: Dio lists the right to enact any laws he might wish and to call them leges Augustae.
dispute: Only Dio mentions leges Augustae; Augustus' reference to his laws at RG 8.5 gives no hint; the notes say Suetonius was misled (Aug. 27.5).

text: Most scholars read another grant in Dio's list as the consular power for life.
dispute: The page calls the question controversial; there is no explicit statement but Dio's, and the page reads Dio differently.

text: Dio wrote that 'the power of the consuls he took for life', to the extent of using the twelve fasces always and everywhere and 'sitting on a magisterial chair between the consuls at any time'.
dispute: The page reads this as an honour, not a power; most scholars read it as the consular power for life.

text: Augustus reported revisions of the Senate list carried out 'by consular power'.
dispute: The page takes this to mean grants made for each occasion, not a permanent power.

text: In 18 BC Augustus' provincia ran out.
It was renewed for five years.
Agrippa's proconsular imperium was renewed for the same five years.
Agrippa received the tribunician power for five years.
Agrippa's imperium was not made maius until 15 BC.
He proposed his statutes to the people by virtue of his tribunician power, so that they were leges Iuliae.
The consuls, the two chief magistrates elected each year, of 16 BC were young nobles.
The consuls of the years that followed were also young nobles.
Both consuls of 16 BC were related to Augustus.
For the second half of the year 16 BC, the plebeian Lucius Tarius Rufus took over from P. Scipio.
dispute: The page says the reason for the change is not known.

text: Rome was left to the consuls, plus Titus Statilius Taurus as 'prefect of the city and Italy', the official left in charge of the city and Italy.
dispute: The notes say Dio's Greek implies that title, and that it was probably a formal, even if not a standing, office.

text: Agrippa exercised imperial policy in half the empire as collega imperii, a colleague in rule over the empire.
The stepsons could have neither triumph nor ovation, for they were only legati Augusti, commanders acting as deputies of Augustus.
Their powers were renewed for five years, including Agrippa's tribunician power, the powers of a tribune of the plebs.
Dio stated that the cura morum of Augustus was renewed in 12 BC for five years.
dispute: The page notes that on Dio's own account Augustus had held it for five years from 19 BC, so its renewal should have come two years sooner, and it is unsure Augustus held it at all.

text: In 13 BC Agrippa's imperium was defined as maius.
For a brief span Agrippa and Augustus had equal formal authority as rulers of the Roman world.
In March 12 BC, at a solemn assembly of the Roman people, Augustus became pontifex maximus, the head of the state priesthood.
The former triumvir Lepidus had never been deprived of that priestly office.
There was a revision of the Senate list in 11 BC, performed by virtue of censoria potestas, the power of a censor.
Drusus entered upon his consulship of 9 BC in absence.
A census was completed by consular imperium, a special grant.
Augustus' powers were formally renewed for a further complete decade.
Tiberius was not acknowledged as collega imperii.
Tiberius was consul for the second time in 7 BC.
For twenty years Augustus had insisted on only two consuls a year, barring emergencies.
Augustus divided the year into two halves, with two 'ordinary' consuls followed by two 'suffect' consuls, a system that became regular from 5 BC.
